newsitem.title: USA: As dust settles in Iraq, dollar rally seen fading.
newsitem.headline: As dust settles in Iraq, dollar rally seen fading.

text.p: A brief stampede into dollars after a sudden U.S. bombing of Iraq should have little lasting impact, as currency players retreat from television screens to focus on more crucial economic news on the tape, dealers said.
The dollar has already surrendered its morning gains on the mark and seems to have hit a wall against the yen near a seven-week high at 109.45 reached earlier Tuesday.
"It's over," said one New York trader. "The market got a little excited on a typical flight to quality, but clearly there is no follow-through."
The dollar's modest overnight rally extended a Monday advance as oil prices rose with the news the United Nations would delay the start of Iraqi oil sales to raise funds for food and medicine.
The launch of 27 U.S. cruise missiles toward Iraqi targets overnight following reported Iraqi attacks on Kurdish civilians again propelled the dollar higher.
But given the crippled state of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's once formidable armed forces, currency analysts see little threat of a larger confontation.

"In the past, these kinds of incidents have had only transitory effects," said Chris Iggo, international economist at Barclays Bank. "If it escalates, it could give some extra support to the dollar. If there's no escalation, it will pretty much cool into the background."
Higher oil prices tend to support the dollar, the currency of choice for commodity transactions, by driving up demand for greenbacks, analysts said.
A spike in crude prices after the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait stoked temporary dollar buying, but the current conflict should remain far smaller, analysts said.
"The Gulf War impact was pretty limited. Even if we get a fairly severe escalation here, I doubt we'll see much more," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
A weak U.S. bond market has curtailed the recent dollar rally and the bond slide could steepen when the August U.S. nonfarm payrolls report debuts Friday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
As the fireworks in Iraq abate, the currency market will turn exclusively to more urgent economic news, analysts said.
"Bonds are limiting any upside (dollar) potential in the short-run. If we get a real (bond) meltdown, there will be some risk that the dollar sells off sharply," Gilmore said.
Traders deemed the potential military threat from Iraq quite minor given the vast reduction in its offensive weaponry following the Gulf War.

With the "no-fly" zones within Iraq's own borders tightened even further after its latest incursion and at least partial international support for the U.S. attack, foreign exchange markets have little to fear, dealers said.
"This was quite a lot to come back to after a long weekend and it took a while to figure out the long-term implications," said ond trader. "But there is nothing Saddam (Hussein) can do now."
